question: With what anguish and urgent perplexity does Habakkuk open his prophetic burden in Habakkuk 1:1-2?
opt1: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!"
opt2: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!"
opt3: "Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth!"
opt4: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me?"
correct: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!"
explanation: Habakkuk begins with a bold lament over apparent divine inaction amidst societal violence. Habakkuk 1:1-2 (KJV) - "The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see. O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!"

question: What pervasive breakdown of legal and moral order in Judah does the prophet lament before the LORD in Habakkuk 1:3-4?
opt1: The temple gates are burned, priests offer sacrifices to Moloch, and the royal lineage is cut off
opt2: The law is slacked, judgment never goes forth, the wicked surround the righteous, and perverse judgment proceedeth
opt3: False prophets proclaim peace for silver, the king robs the storehouses, and the poor starve in streets
opt4: The Sabbath is profaned across all tribes, ancient landmarks are removed, and widows are sold into debt slavery
correct: The law is slacked, judgment never goes forth, the wicked surround the righteous, and perverse judgment proceedeth
explanation: Injustice paralyzed Judah's legal system, leaving the righteous defenseless against corrupt oppressors. Habakkuk 1:3-4 (KJV) - "Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and cause me to behold grievance? for spoiling and violence are before me: and there are that raise up strife and contention. Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth."

question: What astonishing divine announcement introduces God's unexpected answer to Habakkuk's lament in Habakkuk 1:5?
opt1: "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the LORD hath spoken; I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me"
opt2: "Call together the solemn assembly, blow the trumpet in Zion: for the day of the LORD is at hand, and who can abide it?"
opt3: "Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days, which ye will not believe, though it be told you"
opt4: "Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee to scatter all thine enemies"
correct: "Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days, which ye will not believe, though it be told you"
explanation: God announces an unbelievable intervention among the nations in the prophet's own days. Habakkuk 1:5 (KJV) - "Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days, which ye will not believe, though it be told you."

question: What ruthless imperial instrument does the LORD declare He is raising up to execute judgment across the earth in Habakkuk 1:6?
opt1: The Assyrians, an iron-fisted empire marching from Nineveh to destroy fortified cities with fire
opt2: The Medes and Persians, a righteous coalition ordained to execute vengeance upon the kings of Canaan
opt3: The Scythians, a fierce equestrian horde sweeping across the northern steppes to strip all vineyards
opt4: The Chaldeans (Babylonians), a bitter and hasty nation marching through the land to seize dwellingplaces not theirs
correct: The Chaldeans (Babylonians), a bitter and hasty nation marching through the land to seize dwellingplaces not theirs
explanation: God sovereignly raises the Chaldeans to possess lands that do not belong to them. Habakkuk 1:6 (KJV) - "For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs."

question: With what terrifying animal metaphors does Habakkuk portray the speed and ferocity of the Chaldean cavalry in Habakkuk 1:8?
opt1: Horses swifter than leopards, more fierce than evening wolves, with horsemen flying like the eagle that hasteth to eat
opt2: War horses roaring like young lions, charging like horned bulls, and leaping upon fortress walls like mountain leopards
opt3: Steeds unbridled like desert stallions, trampling soldiers like wild oxen, and striking like venomous adders
opt4: Cavalry sweeping like ravenous bears in winter, pursuing like desert falcons, and devouring like locust swarms
correct: Horses swifter than leopards, more fierce than evening wolves, with horsemen flying like the eagle that hasteth to eat
explanation: The Babylonian cavalry is compared to swift leopards, fierce twilight wolves, and hungry diving eagles. Habakkuk 1:7-8 (KJV) - "They are terrible and dreadful: their judgment and their dignity shall proceed of themselves. Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves: and their horsemen shall spread themselves, and their horsemen shall come from far; they shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat."

question: How do the Chaldeans treat royal monarchs and fortified strongholds during their relentless conquest in Habakkuk 1:10?
opt1: They execute captured kings with bronze swords and burn all citadels with sulfur before dawn
opt2: They scoff at kings, hold princes in scorn, and deride every stronghold by heaping dust to capture it
opt3: They force princes to pay tribute in talents of silver and tunnel beneath ramparts with iron picks
opt4: They bind monarchs in copper fetters and demand that conquered cities surrender their gods
correct: They scoff at kings, hold princes in scorn, and deride every stronghold by heaping dust to capture it
explanation: Chaldean arrogance scoffs at earthly rulers and effortlessly overcomes walled cities with earthen siege ramps. Habakkuk 1:9-10 (KJV) - "They shall come all for violence: their faces shall sup up as the east wind, and they shall gather the captivity as the sand. And they shall scoff at the kings, and the princes shall be a scorn unto them: they shall deride every strong hold; for they shall heap dust, and take it."

question: What grievous spiritual offense and idolatrous hubris will the Babylonian conqueror commit in the climax of his pride in Habakkuk 1:11?
opt1: He will enter the Most Holy Place and place the golden statue of Bel upon the Ark of the Covenant
opt2: He will proclaim himself the eternal creator of heaven and earth, demanding all men worship his image
opt3: His mind will change, he will pass over and offend, imputing this his military power unto his god
opt4: He will melt down the holy vessels of the temple to drink wine during a feast of blasphemy
correct: His mind will change, he will pass over and offend, imputing this his military power unto his god
explanation: The conqueror commits the ultimate sin of attributing his conquests to his false god (or his own power). Habakkuk 1:11 (KJV) - "Then shall his mind change, and he shall pass over, and offend, imputing this his power unto his god."

question: What foundational affirmation of God's eternal nature and covenant preservation does Habakkuk cling to in his second perplexity in Habakkuk 1:12?
opt1: "The LORD our God is one LORD: and he will not cast off his people neither forsake his inheritance for the heathen"
opt2: "Thou art the Rock of ages, in whose shadow we abide: and no weapon formed against Zion shall ever prosper"
opt3: "Righteous art thou, O LORD, when I plead with thee: yet let me talk with thee of thy judgments upon Jerusalem"
opt4: "Art thou not from everlasting, O LORD my God, mine Holy One? we shall not die. O LORD, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O mighty God, thou hast established them for correction"
correct: "Art thou not from everlasting, O LORD my God, mine Holy One? we shall not die. O LORD, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O mighty God, thou hast established them for correction"
explanation: Habakkuk anchors himself in Yahweh's eternity and holiness, recognizing Babylon is an instrument of chastisement, not final destruction. Habakkuk 1:12 (KJV) - "Art thou not from everlasting, O LORD my God, mine Holy One? we shall not die. O LORD, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O mighty God, thou hast established them for correction."

question: What profound theological dilemma (theodicy) does the prophet present to God regarding His immaculate holiness and the wicked Babylonians?
opt1: "Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?"
opt2: "How can the Judge of all the earth slay the righteous with the wicked, that the righteous should be as the wicked?"
opt3: "Why standest thou afar off, O LORD? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble when the proud persecuteth the poor?"
opt4: "Shall not the Almighty render unto every man according to his deeds, rather than giving the kingdom to idolatrous nations?"
correct: "Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?"
explanation: Habakkuk wrestles with how an all-holy God can use a far more wicked pagan nation to swallow up Judah. Habakkuk 1:13 (KJV) - "Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?"

question: With what fishing metaphor does Habakkuk depict the helpless subjugation of nations and the conqueror's self-deifying idolatry in Habakkuk 1:14-16?
opt1: Nations gathered like sheep into pens by night, while the shepherds sell the fleece to foreign merchants for gold
opt2: Men made like leaderless fishes caught in hooks and drag-nets, while the fishermen sacrifice and burn incense to their nets because their portion is fat
opt3: Peoples hunted like wild gazelles into pits, while the archers offer the horns upon altars of blood
opt4: Tribes reaped like barley into bundles, while the harvesters bow down to their iron sickles in the fields
correct: Men made like leaderless fishes caught in hooks and drag-nets, while the fishermen sacrifice and burn incense to their nets because their portion is fat
explanation: Babylon sweeps up helpless humans like ocean fish and worships the military weapons (net and drag) that enrich them. Habakkuk 1:14-16 (KJV) - "And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them? They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad. Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous."

question: Where does Habakkuk position himself to await the divine response to his agonizing theological complaint in Habakkuk 2:1?
opt1: "I will enter into the inner court of the temple, and fall upon my face before the Ark until the glory of the LORD appears"
opt2: "I will go forth into the desolate wilderness of Judah, and sit under a juniper tree until the voice of God speaks"
opt3: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved"
opt4: "I will ascend the heights of Mount Olivet at midnight, and watch the heavens for a sign of divine deliverance"
correct: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved"
explanation: The prophet deliberately assumes a sentinel's watchful stance upon the rampart, waiting expectantly for God's answer. Habakkuk 2:1 (KJV) - "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved."

question: What instructions and encouragement did the LORD give regarding recording and trusting the prophetic vision in Habakkuk 2:2-3?
opt1: Seal up the vision in an earthen jar for seventy years; for it belongs to a distant generation that shall return from exile
opt2: Proclaim the vision with trumpets upon all city walls; for the judgment shall fall within forty days without delay
opt3: Inscribe the vision with an iron pen upon the rock of Horeb; for it shall stand as an eternal witness against Babylon
opt4: Write the vision plainly upon tables that he may run that readeth it; though it tarry, wait for it, for at the end it will speak, not lie, and surely come
correct: Write the vision plainly upon tables that he may run that readeth it; though it tarry, wait for it, for at the end it will speak, not lie, and surely come
explanation: The vision was to be legibly inscribed on tablets for a runner to read, with assurance of fulfillment at its appointed time. Habakkuk 2:2-3 (KJV) - "And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it. For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry."

question: What immortal biblical axiom contrasts the haughty oppressor with the righteous believer in Habakkuk 2:4?
opt1: "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith"
opt2: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God: but the humble shall inherit the blessings of the covenant"
opt3: "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall: but he that walketh uprightly shall abide"
opt4: "The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and shall be exalted in glory"
correct: "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith"
explanation: This landmark verse, foundational to New Testament theology, establishes faith/faithfulness as the principle of true spiritual life. Habakkuk 2:4 (KJV) - "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith."

question: In the First Woe against the insatiable conqueror whose desire is enlarged like hell, what taunting proverb will nations take up against him in Habakkuk 2:6?
opt1: "Woe to the crown of pride, whose glorious beauty is a fading flower upon the head of the fat valleys!"
opt2: "Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay!"
opt3: "Woe to him that heapeth up silver like the dust, and fine gold as the mire of the streets!"
opt4: "Woe to the shepherd that leaveth the flock! the sword shall be upon his arm, and upon his right eye!"
correct: "Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay!"
explanation: The plundering conqueror is burdened down under the pledge of ill-gotten wealth, likened to heavy clay. Habakkuk 2:5-6 (KJV) - "Yea also, because he transgresseth by wine, he is a proud man, neither keepeth at home, who enlargeth his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathereth unto him all nations, and heapeth unto him all people: Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay!"

question: What reciprocal retribution (lex talionis) will overtake the world plunderer according to Habakkuk 2:7-8?
opt1: Fierce armies from the south will besiege his capital, and foreign kings will melt his gold for temple ornaments
opt2: Pestilence will devour his royal palace, and his children will be carried into perpetual bond-service in Egypt
opt3: Creditors will rise suddenly to bite and vex him, and because he spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil him
opt4: A mighty earthquake will swallow his walls, and desert nomads will pasture their camels in his gardens
correct: Creditors will rise suddenly to bite and vex him, and because he spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil him
explanation: The despoiler will be despoiled by his victims because of bloodshed and violence against the land and its people. Habakkuk 2:7-8 (KJV) - "Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them? Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men's blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein."

question: In the Second Woe against building an impregnable eagle's nest through extortion, what inanimate architectural elements cry out in testimony in Habakkuk 2:11?
opt1: "The bronze gates of the palace shall groan, and the marble pillars of the court shall weep in dust"
opt2: "The iron bars of the threshold shall testify, and the cedar rafters of the roof shall announce his doom"
opt3: "The cornerstones of the citadel shall crumble, and the foundations of the tower shall refuse to support him"
opt4: "For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it"
correct: "For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it"
explanation: Even the stones and timber of palaces constructed through violent exploitation cry out in condemnation. Habakkuk 2:9-11 (KJV) - "Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil! Thou hast consulted shame to thy house by cutting off many people, and hast sinned against thy soul. For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it."

question: In the Third Woe against building cities with blood, what glorious global promise contrasts with the vanity of imperial labor in Habakkuk 2:14?
opt1: "For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea"
opt2: "For all the kingdoms of this world shall become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ"
opt3: "For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles"
opt4: "For the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established in the top of the mountains forever"
correct: "For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea"
explanation: While empires labor for fire and vanity, God's eternal purpose is the worldwide reign of His glory. Habakkuk 2:12-14 (KJV) - "Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity! Behold, is it not of the LORD of hosts that the people shall labour in the very fire, and the people shall weary themselves for very vanity? For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea."

question: In the Fourth Woe against intoxicating and humiliating neighbors, what cup does the LORD decree shall be turned back upon the offender in Habakkuk 2:16?
opt1: The cup of burning brimstone and unquenchable sulfur shall be poured into his mouth before all nations
opt2: The cup of the LORD's right hand shall be turned unto him, and shameful spewing shall be on his glory
opt3: The cup of trembling shall be placed into his hand, and he shall be drunken with the fury of the Almighty
opt4: The golden flagon of the king shall be dashed to pieces, and his royal purple stained with bitter gall
correct: The cup of the LORD's right hand shall be turned unto him, and shameful spewing shall be on his glory
explanation: The predator who delighted in stripping others will be made to drink the cup of Yahweh's wrath and suffer shameful vomit on his glory. Habakkuk 2:15-16 (KJV) - "Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness! Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the LORD's right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory."

question: In the Fifth Woe against lifeless idolatry, how does the prophet expose the absurdity of worshipping gilded images in Habakkuk 2:19?
opt1: "Woe unto them that fall down before molten calves, and say to the work of their hands, Ye are our deliverers!"
opt2: "Woe unto him that burneth half of the tree in the fire, and of the residue maketh a graven god to pray unto it!"
opt3: "Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it"
opt4: "Woe unto all makers of idols, for they shall be confounded together: their silver shall be cast into the streets!"
correct: "Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it"
explanation: Nahum mocks the folly of praying 'Awake' to wood and 'Arise' to stone covered in gold but devoid of breath. Habakkuk 2:18-19 (KJV) - "What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols? Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it."

question: With what majestic, reverent proclamation of divine transcendence does Chapter 2 reach its dramatic climax in Habakkuk 2:20?
opt1: "The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof"
opt2: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory"
opt3: "The LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us"
opt4: "But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him"
correct: "But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him"
explanation: In contrast to dead, dumb idols, the living LORD reigns in His heavenly sanctuary, commanding universal cosmic awe and silence. Habakkuk 2:20 (KJV) - "But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him."

question: In the prophet's liturgical prayer upon Shigionoth, what dual petition does Habakkuk present to the LORD in Habakkuk 3:2?
opt1: "O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy"
opt2: "O LORD, hasten thy coming upon the mountains of Zion; in the midst of our distress send the Messiah"
opt3: "O LORD, forgive the transgression of thy heritage; in the day of battle be our shield and exceeding great reward"
opt4: "O LORD, restore the throne of David as in the days of old; in the midst of the heathen make bare thine holy arm"
correct: "O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy"
explanation: Habakkuk pleads for a revival of God's redemptive deeds and for mercy to temper impending wrath. Habakkuk 3:1-2 (KJV) - "A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth. O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy."

question: What celestial theophany portrays the Holy One advancing from the southern desert regions in Habakkuk 3:3-4?
opt1: God descended upon Mount Sinai with thunder and thick cloud, seven trumpets sounded, and angels surrounded His chariot
opt2: God came from Teman and Mount Paran, His glory covered the heavens, brightness was as the light, and rays/horns came out of His hand where power was hidden
opt3: God marched from Mount Zion with a pillar of fire, the sun darkened before Him, and the stars sang together
opt4: God advanced from the Jordan valley with an overflowing river of light, burning sulfur consuming the desert plains
correct: God came from Teman and Mount Paran, His glory covered the heavens, brightness was as the light, and rays/horns came out of His hand where power was hidden
explanation: The divine Warrior advances from Edom/Sinai (Teman and Mount Paran) in dazzling celestial splendor. Habakkuk 3:3-4 (KJV) - "God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. And his brightness was as the light; he had horns coming out of his hand: and there was the hiding of his power."

question: What cosmic dread and trembling shook ancient nomadic lands during God's measuring of the earth in Habakkuk 3:5-7?
opt1: Fierce hailstones battered the trees of Lebanon, the plains of Moab melted, and the princes of Ammon fled into caves
opt2: Great rivers dried up across the Arabah, the walls of Jericho fell, and the kings of the Amorites were smitten with madness
opt3: Pestilence and burning coals went with Him, everlasting mountains scattered, and the tents of Cushan and curtains of Midian trembled
opt4: Locust swarms obscured the desert sun, the wells of Beersheba dried up, and the merchants of Sheba fell on their faces
correct: Pestilence and burning coals went with Him, everlasting mountains scattered, and the tents of Cushan and curtains of Midian trembled
explanation: Nature and surrounding desert tribes (Cushan and Midian) convulsed as the eternal God measured the earth. Habakkuk 3:5-7 (KJV) - "Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals went forth at his feet. He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways are everlasting. I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble."

question: What divine weaponry and redemptive vehicles are unveiled as God marches forward in Habakkuk 3:8-9?
opt1: His iron chariot of judgment, His glittering sword bathed in heaven, scattering sulfur upon the sea
opt2: His two-edged spear of light, His golden shield covering the righteous, shattering the mountains of Canaan
opt3: His celestial army of cherubim, His molten slingstones of wrath, drying up the deep foundations of the earth
opt4: His horses and chariots of salvation, His bow made quite naked according to the oaths of the tribes, cleaving the earth with rivers
correct: His horses and chariots of salvation, His bow made quite naked according to the oaths of the tribes, cleaving the earth with rivers
explanation: God rides victorious chariots of salvation, unveiling His sworn covenant bow to defend His people. Habakkuk 3:8-9 (KJV) - "Was the LORD displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation? Thy bow was made quite naked, according to the oaths of the tribes, even thy word. Selah. Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers."

question: How did celestial bodies and cosmic elements react during God's indignant march to thresh the nations in Habakkuk 3:10-12?
opt1: The deep lifted up his hands, the sun and moon stood still in their habitation at the shining of His glittering spear, as He threshed the heathen in anger
opt2: The stars fell from their courses like unripe figs, the ocean dried into salt, and the moon turned to blood before His chariot
opt3: The clouds dissolved into fiery torrents, the earth split open from Dan to Beersheba, and kings cast their crowns into dust
opt4: The pillars of heaven shook with great thunder, the morning star veiled its face, and all seas fled before His countenance
correct: The deep lifted up his hands, the sun and moon stood still in their habitation at the shining of His glittering spear, as He threshed the heathen in anger
explanation: Echoing Joshua's long day, the sun and moon halted in awe as Yahweh marched forth threshing the heathen. Habakkuk 3:10-12 (KJV) - "The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high. The sun and moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, and at the shining of thy glittering spear. Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger."

question: What central redemptive purpose and decisive victory over the head of the wicked is revealed in Habakkuk 3:13?
opt1: "Thou didst arise to avenge the blood of thy prophets, and didst cast the throne of Babylon into the depths of the sea"
opt2: "Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck"
opt3: "Thou didst lead forth thy flock like sheep by the hand of Moses, and didst shatter the power of the oppressor forever"
opt4: "Thou didst establish the sanctuary on Mount Zion, and didst crown the Son of David with glory and everlasting honor"
correct: "Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck"
explanation: The ultimate purpose of the theophany is the salvation of God's people and His Anointed (Messiah), crushing the head of the wicked house. Habakkuk 3:13 (KJV) - "Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah."

question: How did the LORD turn the enemy's cruel ambush back upon himself during the deliverance in Habakkuk 3:14-15?
opt1: He turned their iron swords against their own ranks, and buried their cavalry beneath an avalanche of burning sulfur
opt2: He struck their archers with blindness so they shot one another, while angels parted the swollen waters of the Euphrates
opt3: He struck through with his own staves the head of his villages when they came out as a whirlwind to scatter, and walked through the sea with His horses
opt4: He caused the earth to open her mouth and swallow their siege engines, while His holy presence calmed the stormy deep
correct: He struck through with his own staves the head of his villages when they came out as a whirlwind to scatter, and walked through the sea with His horses
explanation: God used the enemy's own weapons ('his staves') to pierce the oppressor who gloated over devouring the poor. Habakkuk 3:14-15 (KJV) - "Thou didst strike through with his staves the head of his villages: they came out as a whirlwind to scatter me: their rejoicing was as to devour the poor secretly. Thou didst walk through the sea with thine horses, through the heap of great waters."

question: What intense physical shock overcame Habakkuk upon hearing the divine revelation of the coming Babylonian invasion in Habakkuk 3:16?
opt1: He fell blind to the earth, his voice failed for forty days, and his skin was covered with cold sweat of death
opt2: His heart melted like wax, his joints were loosed, and he tore his hair while sitting in dust and ashes
opt3: His knees smote together, his breath was cut off, and he fled into the caves of Engedi to weep alone
opt4: His belly trembled, his lips quivered, rottenness entered into his bones, and he trembled in himself, waiting to rest in the day of trouble
correct: His belly trembled, his lips quivered, rottenness entered into his bones, and he trembled in himself, waiting to rest in the day of trouble
explanation: The anticipation of the brutal invasion produced physical trembling, quivering lips, and weakened bones. Habakkuk 3:16 (KJV) - "When I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble: when he cometh up unto the people, he will invade them with his troops."

question: With what sublime hymn of triumphant faith in the face of total agricultural catastrophe and famine does Habakkuk rejoice in Habakkuk 3:17-18?
opt1: Although fig tree blossoms not, no fruit in vines, olive labor fails, fields yield no meat, flocks and herds cut off; "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation"
opt2: Though mountains be carried into the midst of the sea, waters roar, and earth shake; "Yet will we not fear, for the LORD of hosts is with us"
opt3: Though our storehouses be emptied by the enemy, our vineyards burned, and our silver stolen; "Yet will we praise the name of our King"
opt4: Though father and mother forsake us, and friends prove false; "Yet the LORD will take us up and feed our souls with heavenly manna"
correct: Although fig tree blossoms not, no fruit in vines, olive labor fails, fields yield no meat, flocks and herds cut off; "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation"
explanation: Even with total loss of crops, olives, and livestock, Habakkuk's joy remains unwavering in the God of his salvation. Habakkuk 3:17-18 (KJV) - "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation."

question: With what inspiring declaration of spiritual agility, strength, and liturgical subscription does the Book of Habakkuk conclude in Habakkuk 3:19?
opt1: "The LORD will give strength unto his people; the LORD will bless his people with peace. To the chief musician upon Neginoth"
opt2: "The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments"
opt3: "The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms. A song of degrees for the sons of Korah"
opt4: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits: who redeemeth thy life from destruction. Selah"
correct: "The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments"
explanation: Habakkuk ends with personal triumph in God, granting him sure-footed hinds' feet to walk upon spiritual heights, dedicated to the chief singer. Habakkuk 3:19 (KJV) - "The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments."
